title: Analytical Applications of Differentiation
overview: This unit turns derivative computations into conclusions about the shape and behavior of a function. You will use the Mean Value Theorem and the Extreme Value Theorem to justify claims, locate and classify extrema with the first derivative test, the candidates test, and the second derivative test, and determine concavity and points of inflection. You will also connect the graphs of a function and its first two derivatives, sketch curves from derivative information, solve optimization word problems, and analyze the behavior of implicitly defined curves.

skills.name: The Mean Value Theorem and the Extreme Value Theorem: hypotheses and conclusions
Critical points and intervals of increase and decrease
The first derivative test and the candidates test for extrema
Concavity, points of inflection, and the second derivative test
Connecting the graphs of f, f', and f'' and sketching curves

lessons.title: The Mean Value Theorem and the Extreme Value Theorem

sections.html:
The Extreme Value Theorem (EVT) states: if a function $f$ is continuous on a closed interval $[a, b]$, then $f$ attains an absolute maximum value and an absolute minimum value somewhere on $[a, b]$. An absolute maximum value is a value $f(c)$ with $f(c) \geq f(x)$ for every $x$ in the interval; the absolute minimum is defined the same way with the inequality reversed.

Both hypotheses are required. On the open interval $(0, 1)$, the continuous function $f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$ has no maximum value: as $x$ moves toward $0$, the values grow without bound. On a closed interval, a function with a jump discontinuity can also fail to attain an extreme value. When the interval is closed and the function is continuous, the EVT guarantees that the extreme values exist; it does not say where they are.

The Mean Value Theorem (MVT) states: if $f$ is continuous on the closed interval $[a, b]$ and differentiable on the open interval $(a, b)$, then there is at least one number $c$ in $(a, b)$ with

$$f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}$$

The right side is the average rate of change of $f$ over $[a, b]$, which is the slope of the secant line through $(a, f(a))$ and $(b, f(b))$. The MVT says the instantaneous rate of change equals that average rate at least once strictly between the endpoints.

Check both hypotheses before using the theorem. Continuity is needed on the closed interval, endpoints included. Differentiability is needed only on the open interval, so a corner at an endpoint does not block the theorem, but a corner at an interior point does.

The special case with $f(a) = f(b)$ is called Rolle's Theorem: the average rate of change is $0$, so some $c$ in $(a, b)$ has $f'(c) = 0$.

The MVT is the statement behind this claim: if a file transfer moves $400$ megabytes in $100$ seconds, then at some instant the instantaneous transfer rate was exactly $4$ megabytes per second. The average rate over the interval must be matched exactly at least once, provided the amount-transferred function is continuous in time and differentiable during the transfer.

Where the analogy holds: the amount transferred as a function of time plays the role of $f$, the average throughput is the secant slope, and the instantaneous rate is $f'$.

Where it breaks: real telemetry is sampled. A discrete sequence of measurements has no MVT. Between two ticks the rate can jump across the average value without ever equaling it, the same way a variable stepping from $3.9$ to $4.1$ never holds the value $4.0$. The theorem needs a genuinely continuous quantity; its proof depends on the completeness of the real numbers, which an array of samples does not have.

sections.title: Find the value $c$ guaranteed by the Mean Value Theorem for $f(x) = x^3$ on $[0, 2]$

steps.text: Check the hypotheses. The polynomial $x^3$ is continuous on $[0, 2]$ and differentiable on $(0, 2)$, so the MVT applies.
Compute the average rate of change over the interval.
Set the derivative equal to the average rate and solve.
Keep only the solution inside the open interval $(0, 2)$; the negative square root is outside.

sections.html:
Two exam-relevant consequences follow.

First, hypothesis failures are testable. The function $f(x) = |x|$ on $[-1, 2]$ is continuous, but it is not differentiable at the interior point $x = 0$, so the MVT does not apply. When a conclusion of the MVT fails for a specific function, the explanation is always a specific failed hypothesis, and the AP exam expects you to name it.

Second, the MVT converts table data into guarantees. If $f$ is differentiable everywhere and a table gives $f(1) = 3$ and $f(4) = 12$, then some $c$ in $(1, 4)$ satisfies $f'(c) = \frac{12 - 3}{4 - 1} = 3$. A complete justification names the theorem and states that its hypotheses hold: continuity on the closed interval and differentiability on the open interval.

lessons.title: Critical points and intervals of increase and decrease

sections.html:
A critical point of a function $f$ is a number $c$ in the domain of $f$ where $f'(c) = 0$ or $f'(c)$ does not exist. Critical points are the only interior locations where a relative maximum or minimum can occur; this fact is the reason the tests in this unit examine critical points first.

Both parts of the definition matter. For $f(x) = x^{2/3}$, the derivative $f'(x) = \frac{2}{3}x^{-1/3}$ is undefined at $x = 0$, and $x = 0$ is in the domain of $f$, so $x = 0$ is a critical point; the graph has a minimum there with no horizontal tangent. For $f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$, the derivative is undefined at $x = 0$, but $0$ is not in the domain of $f$, so it is not a critical point.

A critical point is a candidate, not a conclusion. The function $f(x) = x^3$ has $f'(0) = 0$, and $x = 0$ is neither a maximum nor a minimum.

On an interval, if $f'(x) > 0$ for every $x$ in the interval, then $f$ is increasing there; if $f'(x) < 0$ throughout, $f$ is decreasing. The standard procedure, called a sign chart, is:

  1. Compute $f'$ and factor it.
  2. Find all critical points and any domain breaks; these cut the number line into intervals.
  3. Determine the sign of $f'$ on each interval, either by testing one point or by reading the signs of the factors.
  4. Conclude: increasing where $f'$ is positive, decreasing where $f'$ is negative.

The sign of $f'$ can only change at a critical point or a domain break, so one test point per interval is enough. A factor with an even exponent, such as $(x-1)^2$, is nonnegative everywhere, so $f'$ does not change sign at its zero; checking for the sign change instead of assuming it prevents a common error.

A sign chart is interval partitioning followed by constant propagation. The zeros of $f'$ partition the number line into segments, and within one segment the predicate fprime(x) > 0 evaluates to the same boolean for every $x$, so you evaluate it once per segment, like caching a pure function's result for an entire equivalence class of inputs. That is why one test point per interval suffices.

Where the analogy holds exactly: the partition boundaries are precisely the places the boolean can flip, namely zeros of $f'$ and domain breaks, the way a piecewise-constant config value can only change at declared boundaries.

Where it breaks: the guarantee comes from the Intermediate Value Theorem applied to a continuous $f'$, not from any programming principle. If $f'$ has a discontinuity you did not include as a boundary, the cached boolean can be wrong inside a segment. The mathematics forces you to enumerate the boundaries correctly; there is no runtime check that catches a missed one.

sections.title: Intervals of increase and decrease for $f(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 12x$

steps.text: Differentiate and factor.
Set $f'(x) = 0$. The critical points are $x = -1$ and $x = 2$, which cut the line into three intervals.
Test the sign of $f'$ on each interval.
Conclude from the signs.

sections.html:
Critical points from an undefined derivative appear with roots, fractional exponents, and absolute values. Work them the same way: the points where $f'$ is zero or undefined, together with domain breaks, are the interval boundaries for the sign chart.

For products with exponentials, remember that $e^{u}$ is positive for every real $u$, so a factor of $e^{-x}$ never contributes a zero or a sign change. For $f(x) = x e^{-x}$, the derivative $f'(x) = e^{-x}(1 - x)$ is zero only where $1 - x = 0$.

lessons.title: Classifying extrema: the first derivative test and the candidates test

sections.html:
The first derivative test classifies a critical point $c$ of a continuous function by the sign of $f'$ on each side:

  • If $f'$ changes from positive to negative at $c$, then $f$ has a relative maximum at $c$: the function rises into the point and falls after it.
  • If $f'$ changes from negative to positive at $c$, then $f$ has a relative minimum at $c$.
  • If $f'$ has the same sign on both sides of $c$, then $f$ has no relative extremum at $c$.

A relative maximum (also called a local maximum) at $c$ means $f(c) \geq f(x)$ for all $x$ near $c$; it is a statement about a neighborhood, not about the whole domain.

The sign change is the substance of the test. A critical point where $f'$ does not change sign, such as $x = 0$ for $f(x) = x^3$, is not an extremum.

sections.title: Classify the critical points of $f(x) = x^4 - 2x^2$

steps.text: Differentiate and factor completely.
The critical points are $x = -1$, $x = 0$, and $x = 1$. Build the sign chart with one test point per interval.

Apply the first derivative test at each critical point: negative to positive at $x = -1$ gives a relative minimum; positive to negative at $x = 0$ gives a relative maximum; negative to positive at $x = 1$ gives a relative minimum.
Report the function values when the question asks for them.

sections.html:
An absolute maximum of $f$ on an interval is the largest value $f$ attains anywhere on that interval. On a closed interval $[a, b]$, the EVT guarantees that a continuous function attains an absolute maximum and minimum, and calculus narrows down where: at a critical point in the interior or at an endpoint. This yields the candidates test, also called the closed interval method:

  1. Find all critical points of $f$ inside $(a, b)$.
  2. Evaluate $f$ at each interior critical point and at both endpoints $a$ and $b$.
  3. The largest of these values is the absolute maximum; the smallest is the absolute minimum.

Two details. First, the test compares function values, so the answer to a value question is $f(c)$, not $c$; read whether the question asks for the value or for its location. Second, no sign analysis is needed for the candidates test. Evaluating and comparing is sufficient, because the EVT guarantees the winner is in the candidate list.

The candidates test reduces a search over infinitely many points to a maximum over a small array. Calculus proves the absolute extremum of a continuous function on $[a, b]$ must occur at a critical point or an endpoint, so you collect those finitely many candidates, map $f$ over them, and take the largest, like replacing a brute-force scan with a proof that only a few indices can hold the answer. The comparison step really is just candidates.map(f) followed by Math.max; there is no further calculus in it.

Where the analogy breaks: the reduction is valid only under the theorem's hypotheses. On an open or unbounded interval, or for a discontinuous $f$, the extremum may fail to exist at all, and the candidate list proves nothing, the way an index-based shortcut becomes invalid once the array invariant it relies on is broken. In those cases you must analyze the boundary or limiting behavior directly.

steps.text: Find the interior critical points.
Both critical points lie inside $(-1, 5)$, so the candidate list is $x = -1, 0, 4, 5$.
Evaluate $f$ at every candidate.
Compare. The absolute maximum value is $5$ at $x = 0$; the absolute minimum value is $-27$ at $x = 4$.

lessons.title: Concavity, points of inflection, and the second derivative test

sections.html:
A differentiable function is concave up on an interval when its derivative $f'$ is increasing there, and concave down when $f'$ is decreasing. Geometrically, concave up means the graph bends upward and lies above its tangent lines; concave down means it bends downward and lies below them.

When $f''$ exists, the practical test is the sign of the second derivative: $f''(x) > 0$ on an interval means concave up; $f''(x) < 0$ means concave down. The procedure mirrors the increasing and decreasing sign chart, one derivative higher: compute $f''$, find where it is zero or undefined, and test the sign on each resulting interval.

Concavity and direction are independent properties. A function can be increasing and concave down at the same time: rising, but at a slowing rate.

A point of inflection is a point on the graph where concavity changes, which means $f''$ changes sign there. The condition $f''(c) = 0$ alone is not sufficient. For $f(x) = x^4$, the second derivative $f''(x) = 12x^2$ is zero at $x = 0$ but positive on both sides, so concavity does not change and there is no inflection point.

The working procedure: solve $f''(x) = 0$, note where $f''$ is undefined, then verify that the sign of $f''$ actually changes across each candidate. Report an inflection point with both coordinates when the question asks for the point rather than the $x$-value.

For a metric sampled over time, $f$ is the value, $f'$ is the rate of change, and $f''$ is the change in that rate, the second difference of the series. An error count rising means $f'$ is positive; the count rising ever faster means $f''$ is positive too. A point of inflection is the moment a growth curve switches from speeding up to slowing down, which is the signal you watch when deciding whether an incident is getting worse or beginning to recover, even while the raw count is still climbing.

Where the analogy holds: the sign of the first difference tracks direction, the sign of the second difference tracks curvature, and the two are independent, exactly as with $f'$ and $f''$.

Where it breaks: differencing amplifies noise, and a discrete second difference can flip sign on jitter alone. The mathematical objects $f'$ and $f''$ are exact; production dashboards approximate them with smoothing, and the smoothing window changes where the apparent inflection point lands.

The second derivative test classifies a critical point using concavity. Suppose $f'(c) = 0$ and $f''$ exists near $c$:

  • If $f''(c) > 0$, the graph is concave up at $c$, so $f$ has a relative minimum at $c$.
  • If $f''(c) < 0$, the graph is concave down at $c$, so $f$ has a relative maximum at $c$.
  • If $f''(c) = 0$, the test is inconclusive: the point may be a maximum, a minimum, or neither. Fall back to the first derivative test.

A literal memory anchor: concave up at a flat point means the graph opens upward around it, which is the shape of a minimum.

The two tests are interchangeable when both apply. The second derivative test is often faster when $f''$ is easy to evaluate; the first derivative test is more general, because it needs no second derivative and it gives a definite answer at any isolated critical point of a continuous function.

sections.title: Classify the critical points of $f(x) = x^3 - 6x^2 + 9x + 1$ and find its inflection point

steps.text: Find the critical points.
Compute the second derivative and evaluate it at each critical point.
Apply the second derivative test: $f''(1) = -6$ is negative, so $x = 1$ is a relative maximum with $f(1) = 5$; $f''(3) = 6$ is positive, so $x = 3$ is a relative minimum with $f(3) = 1$.
Locate the inflection point: $f''(x) = 6x - 12$ changes sign from negative to positive at $x = 2$, and $f(2) = 3$, so the inflection point is $(2, 3)$.

lessons.title: Connecting the graphs of f, f', and f'', with implicit relations

sections.html:
Many AP questions show the graph of $f'$ and ask about $f$. The translations are fixed; read them as a table.

Behavior of $f$Statement about $f'$Statement about $f''$
increasing$f'$ positiveno constraint
decreasing$f'$ negativeno constraint
relative extremum$f'$ zero and changing signno constraint
concave up$f'$ increasing$f''$ positive
concave down$f'$ decreasing$f''$ negative
point of inflection$f'$ has a relative extremum$f''$ zero and changing sign

The most common misread is treating the graph of $f'$ as if it were the graph of $f$. When the graph on the page is $f'$, height means slope of $f$: where the curve on the page is above the axis, $f$ rises; where the curve on the page peaks, $f$ has its steepest rise, not a maximum.

Reading the graph of $f'$ to answer questions about $f$ is working one level of indirection away from the data, like reconstructing a counter from a log of its deltas. A log entry (the value of $f'$) being positive means the counter went up at that moment; the entries themselves trending downward means the counter's growth is slowing, which is concave down, even while every entry is still positive.

Where the analogy holds: it is exact for direction claims, and summing the deltas recovers the counter up to its starting value, matching the fact that $f'$ determines $f$ only up to a constant.

Where it breaks: a delta log is a discrete sum, so it cannot distinguish a smooth change within one tick from a jump, and it has no notion of the differentiability the calculus statements require. Also, reconstructing exact values of $f$ needs the initial value; graph-reading questions about increase, extrema, and concavity deliberately avoid needing it.

steps.text: First derivative: critical points and direction.

The sign of $f'$ is positive, negative, positive across the three intervals, so $f$ increases on $(-\infty, -1)$, decreases on $(-1, 1)$, and increases on $(1, \infty)$. The first derivative test gives a relative maximum at $x = -1$ and a relative minimum at $x = 1$.
Second derivative: concavity and inflection.

Assemble the sketch: the graph rises to $(-1, 3)$, falls through the inflection point $(0, 1)$ while switching from concave down to concave up, reaches $(1, -1)$, then rises. End behavior is that of $x^3$: downward to the left, upward to the right.

sections.html:
The same analysis applies to implicitly defined relations. From implicit differentiation, $\frac{dy}{dx}$ is typically a quotient in $x$ and $y$. On the curve:

  • The tangent is horizontal where the numerator is $0$ and the denominator is not $0$.
  • The tangent is vertical where the denominator is $0$ and the numerator is not $0$.

To locate such points, set the appropriate part of the quotient to zero, combine that condition with the original equation, and solve the system. Every candidate must satisfy the original equation; a pair $(x, y)$ that satisfies the tangency condition but not the curve equation is not a point of the curve.

For concavity, differentiate $\frac{dy}{dx}$ again with respect to $x$, remembering that $y$ and $\frac{dy}{dx}$ both depend on $x$; then substitute the point's coordinates and the already-computed value of $\frac{dy}{dx}$. At a point with a horizontal tangent, the sign of $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ classifies the point exactly as the second derivative test does for explicit functions.

sections.title: Horizontal tangent points of $x^2 - xy + y^2 = 9$

steps.text: Differentiate both sides with respect to $x$; the $xy$ term needs the product rule.
Solve for the derivative.
Horizontal tangents require the numerator to vanish, so $y = 2x$. Substitute into the curve equation.
The candidate points are $(\sqrt{3}, 2\sqrt{3})$ and $(-\sqrt{3}, -2\sqrt{3})$. Check the denominator: $2y - x = 3x$, which is nonzero at both points, so both are genuine horizontal tangent points.

sections.html:
An optimization problem asks for the largest or smallest possible value of a quantity subject to a constraint. A reliable procedure:

  1. Name the variables and describe the configuration.
  2. Write the objective: the quantity to maximize or minimize, as a formula.
  3. Write the constraint: the equation the variables must satisfy.
  4. Use the constraint to rewrite the objective as a function of one variable.
  5. Determine the domain that makes physical sense: lengths nonnegative, quantities within their stated limits.
  6. Find the critical points of the one-variable objective and classify or compare, using the candidates test on a closed domain or a derivative test on an open one.
  7. Answer the question actually asked: the optimizing input, the optimal value, or both.

Step 7 is a real error source. After solving for $x$, reread the problem to see whether it asks for $x$, for another dimension, or for the optimal value of the objective.

An optimization word problem is a small constrained-optimization program. The constraint is an equality you use to eliminate a variable by direct substitution, the way you would inline a definition to reduce a two-parameter function to one parameter. The calculus step then finds the exact argmax of the one-parameter function by solving $f'(x) = 0$, where a numeric approach would run a solver or a grid search.

Where the analogy holds: the domain restriction in step 5 is input validation, and skipping it produces the same class of bug, an optimum at a physically impossible input such as a negative side length.

Where it breaks: gradient-based numeric optimizers can stop at any local optimum, and their answer depends on the starting point. The calculus method enumerates every critical point, so, combined with endpoint checks, it certifies the global optimum on the interval, a guarantee no local search gives. The cost is that it only works when you can differentiate and solve symbolically.

sections.title: Maximum area with $120$ meters of fence and one unfenced side

steps.text: A rectangular field borders a straight river; the river side needs no fence, and the other three sides use $120$ meters of fencing. Let $x$ be the length in meters of each side perpendicular to the river; the constraint makes the parallel side $120 - 2x$.
The physical domain is $0 \leq x \leq 60$; outside it, some side length is negative. Both endpoints give area $0$.
Find the critical point.
Classify: $A''(x) = -4$ is negative everywhere, so $x = 30$ gives the maximum, and the endpoint areas are $0$, confirming it is absolute.
Answer with the asked quantities: the dimensions are $30$ meters by $60$ meters.

The distance from a point $(x, x^2)$ on the parabola to $(0, 3)$ is the objective. Minimize the squared distance $S$; it avoids the square root and has the same minimizer, because squaring is increasing on nonnegative inputs.
Differentiate and factor.
The critical points are $x = 0$ and $x = \pm\sqrt{5/2}$. Compare values of $S$.
The minimum squared distance is $\frac{11}{4}$, so the closest points are $\left(\pm\sqrt{5/2}, \frac{5}{2}\right)$ and the minimum distance is $\frac{\sqrt{11}}{2}$.

questions.prompt: Let $f(x) = x^2$ on the interval $[1, 3]$. Find the value of $c$ whose existence is guaranteed by the Mean Value Theorem.
choices: No such $c$ is guaranteed, because the hypotheses fail
misconceptions: This is the average rate of change $\frac{f(3)-f(1)}{3-1} = 4$ itself; the MVT asks for the $c$ where $f'(c)$ equals that value, so the equation to solve is $2c = 4$.
This comes from setting $f(c)$ equal to the average of $f(1)$ and $f(3)$; the MVT matches the derivative $f'(c)$ to the average rate of change, not $f(c)$ to an average of values.
The hypotheses do not fail: $x^2$ is continuous on the closed interval and differentiable on the open interval, so the MVT applies and produces at least one $c$.
hints: Start by computing the average rate of change of $f$ over $[1, 3]$: the slope of the secant line between the endpoints.
Set $f'(c) = 2c$ equal to the average rate of change you computed and solve for $c$. Confirm the solution lies in the open interval $(1, 3)$.

solution.text: Compute the average rate of change over the interval.
Set the derivative equal to this value.
Solve and check membership in the open interval: $c = 2$ lies in $(1, 3)$.

questions.prompt: A function $f$ is defined on the closed interval $[a, b]$. Which pair of hypotheses is exactly what the Mean Value Theorem requires before it guarantees a $c$ in $(a, b)$ with $f'(c) = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$?
choices: $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and differentiable on $(a, b)$
$f$ is continuous on $(a, b)$ and differentiable on $[a, b]$
$f$ is differentiable on $(a, b)$; continuity is not required
$f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and $f(a) = f(b)$
misconceptions: This swaps the two interval types. Continuity is needed up to and including the endpoints, while differentiability is needed only strictly between them; the MVT does not require one-sided derivatives at $a$ and $b$.
Differentiability on $(a, b)$ gives continuity only on the open interval; the theorem also needs continuity at the endpoints $a$ and $b$, which this choice omits.

The condition $f(a) = f(b)$ belongs to Rolle's Theorem, the special case whose conclusion is $f'(c) = 0$; the MVT works for any endpoint values but still needs differentiability on $(a, b)$, which this choice omits.
hints: One hypothesis is about the closed interval including endpoints; the other is about the open interval strictly between them. Match each property to the correct interval type.
Differentiability at the endpoints themselves is never required, and continuity must extend all the way to the endpoints. Also recall which theorem has the extra condition $f(a) = f(b)$.

solution.text: The MVT hypotheses are: continuity on the closed interval $[a, b]$ and differentiability on the open interval $(a, b)$.
Continuity must include the endpoints because the secant slope uses $f(a)$ and $f(b)$; differentiability is only needed strictly inside, where the guaranteed $c$ lives.
The condition $f(a) = f(b)$ is not an MVT hypothesis; it defines the special case known as Rolle's Theorem.

questions.prompt: Let $f(x) = x^3 - 3x$ on $[0, 3]$. Find the value of $c$ in $(0, 3)$ that satisfies the conclusion of the Mean Value Theorem. Round to three decimal places.
hints: Compute $f(0)$ and $f(3)$, then form the average rate of change $\frac{f(3)-f(0)}{3-0}$.
Set $f'(c) = 3c^2 - 3$ equal to the average rate of change and solve. Keep the root that lies inside $(0, 3)$.

solution.text: Evaluate the endpoints.
Form the average rate of change.
Set the derivative equal to it and solve.
Only the positive root lies in $(0, 3)$.

questions.prompt: On $[0, 3]$, the function $f(x) = |x - 1|$ has average rate of change $\frac{f(3)-f(0)}{3-0} = \frac{2-1}{3} = \frac{1}{3}$, yet there is no $c$ with $f'(c) = \frac{1}{3}$, because $f'$ takes only the values $-1$ and $1$. Which statement explains why this does not contradict the Mean Value Theorem?
choices: $f$ is not differentiable at $x = 1$, so the MVT hypotheses are not satisfied on this interval
$f$ is not continuous at $x = 1$, so the MVT hypotheses are not satisfied on this interval
The MVT requires $f(a) = f(b)$, which fails here
The MVT applies only to functions that are increasing on the whole interval
misconceptions: This confuses the corner with a break: $|x - 1|$ is continuous at every real number. What fails at the corner $x = 1$ is differentiability, because the one-sided slopes $-1$ and $1$ disagree.
The condition $f(a) = f(b)$ is the hypothesis of Rolle's Theorem, not of the MVT; the MVT applies to any endpoint values when its continuity and differentiability hypotheses hold.
The MVT has no monotonicity hypothesis; it applies to functions that rise, fall, or both. The failed hypothesis here is differentiability at the interior point $x = 1$.
hints: The MVT has exactly two hypotheses. Test each one against this specific function on this interval.
Consider the point $x = 1$, where the graph of $|x - 1|$ has a corner. Decide which property a corner destroys: continuity or differentiability.

solution.text: The MVT requires continuity on $[0, 3]$ and differentiability on $(0, 3)$.
$f(x) = |x - 1|$ is continuous everywhere, so the continuity hypothesis holds.

At $x = 1$, the slope from the left is $-1$ and from the right is $1$, so $f'(1)$ does not exist. Since $1$ is inside $(0, 3)$, the differentiability hypothesis fails, and the MVT makes no promise for this function on this interval.

questions.prompt:
The function $f$ is continuous on $[0, 8]$ and differentiable on $(0, 8)$, with selected values given in the table.

$x$$0$$3$$5$$8$
$f(x)$$2$$8$$8$$4$

Consider the statements:

  • I. There is a $c$ in $(0, 8)$ with $f'(c) = \frac{1}{4}$.
  • II. There is a $c$ in $(3, 5)$ with $f'(c) = 0$.
  • III. $f$ attains an absolute maximum value on $[0, 8]$.

Which statements must be true?
misconceptions: Statements II and III also follow: applying the MVT on $[3, 5]$, where the average rate of change is $\frac{8-8}{2} = 0$, gives II, and the Extreme Value Theorem on the closed interval gives III.
Statement II also follows: on $[3, 5]$ the average rate of change is $\frac{8-8}{2} = 0$, so the MVT guarantees a $c$ in $(3, 5)$ with $f'(c) = 0$.
Statement I also follows: on $[0, 8]$ the average rate of change is $\frac{4-2}{8-0} = \frac{1}{4}$, so the MVT guarantees the required $c$.
hints: Test statement I with the MVT applied to the full interval $[0, 8]$: compute the average rate of change from the table.
For statement II, apply the MVT to the subinterval $[3, 5]$ and use the two equal table values.
For statement III, identify the theorem whose only hypotheses are continuity and a closed interval.

solution.text: Statement I: the average rate of change on $[0, 8]$ is $\frac{4 - 2}{8 - 0} = \frac{1}{4}$; the MVT hypotheses hold there, so some $c$ in $(0, 8)$ has $f'(c) = \frac{1}{4}$. True.
Statement II: on $[3, 5]$ the hypotheses also hold, and the average rate of change is $\frac{8 - 8}{5 - 3} = 0$, so some $c$ in $(3, 5)$ has $f'(c) = 0$. True.
Statement III: $f$ is continuous on the closed interval $[0, 8]$, so the Extreme Value Theorem guarantees an absolute maximum. True.
All three statements must be true.

questions.prompt: Find all critical points of $f(x) = x^3 - 12x$.
misconceptions: Solving $3x^2 - 12 = 0$ gives $x^2 = 4$, which has two real solutions; this choice keeps only the positive square root and drops $x = -2$.
This is where $f''(x) = 6x$ equals zero, a candidate for an inflection point; critical points come from $f'(x) = 3x^2 - 12$.
These are the zeros of $f$ itself, from solving $x^3 - 12x = 0$; critical points are zeros of the derivative $f'$, not of $f$.
hints: A critical point of this polynomial is a solution of $f'(x) = 0$. Start by computing $f'$.

questions.prompt: The derivative of a function $f$ is $f'(x) = (x + 2)(x - 1)^2(x - 3)$. At how many values of $x$ does $f$ have a relative extremum?

solution.text: The zeros of $f'$ are $x = -2$, $x = 1$ (from a squared factor), and $x = 3$. Test signs: $f'(-3) = (-1)(16)(-6)$ is positive; $f'(0) = (2)(1)(-3)$ is negative; $f'(2) = (4)(1)(-1)$ is negative; $f'(4) = (6)(9)(1)$ is positive.
Sign changes: positive to negative at $x = -2$ (relative maximum), no change at $x = 1$, negative to positive at $x = 3$ (relative minimum).

Rising then falling at a point where $f$ is continuous is the first derivative test pattern for a relative maximum. The test says nothing about the whole domain, so no absolute claim follows.

At $x = 3$: $f'$ is positive on both sides, so $f$ is increasing before and after; the graph flattens momentarily but has no extremum there.

At $x = 2$, $f''$ changes from negative to positive, so concavity changes from down to up: a point of inflection, regardless of the value of $f'(2)$.
